Bah, I'm not the biggest fan of millenials, but this article seems to be reaching here. i think IT work is getting more stressful as it's becoming more of a commodity. IT workers used to be valued by organizations for their training, skill and expertise. Over the last 6 or 8 years, I've been watching IT workers being treated more and more like faceless cogs in a machine, that management thinks they can replace on a whim. This leads to long hours, lower pay, less benefits and more stress. Management doesn't care about the individual in IT anymore - you're just a replaceable piece of the machine, to be dropped the second you start squeaking.

I would suggest that goes to all areas of business, not just IT.

Did you notice in the last couple of paragraphs where the IT company owner said his older workers could handle the stress better? He explained that it was because the older workers were more experienced....they used to feel more stressed but over time became able to handle the work. The millenials will get there too...they just need time to learn to balance things.

I've been in IT for close to a decade.. The issue is entirely that people refuse to think for themselves. Not that they cant. Not that they are stupid. They just refuse to think for themselves.

Here is an example from...today.

Steve emails us saying he cannot log into application X.

I confirm his profile and account are correct and send Steve a new password and login credentials for him to try and explain that upon using the password it will prompt him to create a new one.

He replies back saying "it did not work, I still not get into application X."

I reply to him asking for a screen shot of what he is seeing.

He replies back with a photo he took with his cell phone. In the screenshot, it is pretty evident the issue is that he does not have internet, as the error message on his screen is simply the "page not found" error message.

I send a tech over to figure out how he managed to disconnect his computer from the net(we run wyse terminals so it basically is just a keyboard/mouse/monitor and a little box). That gets sorted out.

Now, I know Steve. He is probably one of the smartest people I have ever met and does amazing things with the software he was trying to access. He simply didnt take the fucking time to actually look at the error message.

I get that pretty much all day. And I work for the government so it is almost entirely just millennials. Last week I had a lady that was at least 800 years old ask me if I knew why the drivers on her linux system were no longer available.

I have been an IT guy for the last 15 years, working since the middle of the last IT boom in 2001.

It is definitely getting more stressful which is why I have dropped out of the field all together, and am re training in Electronic Engineering

Here is the laundry list of reasons that I and others I have spoken too are dropping the field

  • Pay is going backwards. Jobs that used to pay 35$ an hr are now playing 25$ / hr
  • IT departments everywhere are constantly under staffed and over worked. The average User / Support tech ratio creeping up to be 500+ users Per tech

  • There is an expectation of 50+ hr work weeks and then expecting your to be "on call " after hours, with no extra pay for being "on call." On call destroys your social life and limits what you can do after work. You essentially have to always have your phone on, and be no more than 30 mins from a PC you can use for work.

  • Companies are expecting employees to keep up with ALL the certs, in their own time, off their own back. The cost of that is brutal.. for example

MSCE = 10 exams * $300 Per exam = $3000

CCNA = 2 exams * $400 = $800

VM ware course = $3000

ITIL Certs = $2000

And so on and so on..

You have to re cert about every 5 years in various technologies so that's about another 1k a year of your own money you have to piss away

  • IT budgets are crap, with most places expecting you to build the best solution for half the cost it should take to do it properly, and they it's YOUR arse on the line when it all goes wrong, not the management types who wouldn't sign off on the proper solution budget.
  • Constant threat of being outsourced or your job being kicked over to "the cloud"
  • No budget/resources for IT Security, but when they place gets hacked and owned, you're the one they throw to the wolves.
  • No respect from senior management who sees you as a cost sink, rather than a critical part of keeping their business running.

That's just the short list....

I've been doing IT work since the 80's. You hit a lot of the point I make at least monthly, but the big one is even more simple. In the 80's and 90's companies realized that hiring a person and building his talents, AND KEEPING HIM, was cheaper than hiring and training every few years. Now, they have offloaded all the so called 'perks' onto the employees and know that they can hire a desperate kid right out of tech school for $15 an hour and hire a contractor to do the serious stuff when it all blows up. This is cheaper month to month, but not long term.

My first job they worked me like a dog, but they paid for my certs and training, demanded we all have down time and at least once a year let us work in a new tech into the business as a way to push tech and IT forward. We were vital in training the execs and managers in using everything from cell phones to excel to increase productivity and utilizing the tech we had/wanted into the business. IT was a critical partner in every department; my boss at the time was on the budgeting committee and worked to use tech to save money and make the employees we had more productive and more valuable. I worked there 10 years until a whole new management team came in after a merger and cut off my teams training budget before they even met us. I took the members of the team worth keeping to a new company who understood what a good IT department is worth.

I'm at the point where I do not do the work any more. Management does that to you. Now I look for people who deserve that foot in the door, those kids who will work, learn and grow, and then leave when the company lets the talent go because they need to save $10 this month to meet metrics. It is terribly angry to see companies, both mine and my wife's as an example, not put the investment into long term goals, or into growing their work force like they used to.

Workers are disposable now. You kids coming out of college, should think about what that means. Changing companies every 3-5 years to get a raise will be the norm. Make friends, don't piss people off, remember that high level IT is a closed knit group who all know and google each other. Save to get your certs and keep them current. The observation about millenial users is pretty insightful. The issue there isn't that they're "avid users expecting more service" but rather that they lack communication skills. IT is absolutely dependent on solid communication, particular written.

Further, the article ignores the big change - IT has now become much more central to core business operations. The IT staff who are responsible for a down system are now frequently responsible for a closed store and a disabled workforce. If people simply cannot do their jobs at all when there is an IT issue you can bet IT will be stressed out. This is a far more common situation in the past five years than it was fifteen years ago.

Ok so this is an embarrassing question, but what exactly is IT work. I know a lot of people who say "I work in IT", but to me this is such a broad term that it's like saying I work in the Service Industry, or Healthcare Industry, there could be 1,000s of possibilities. I know it stands for information technology, but what exactly do you guys do. Are you running servers, tech support, computer repair, programming, designing, or all of the above? Thank to however clarifies this for me.

I write budgets for the IT department for the company I work for. I can try to answer this from my recent adventures.

Servers, physical computer hardware, virtual servers and the things that most people think about when they see a "server room" in a tv or movie show.

The software that runs on those servers including licensing, patching, compatibility tables, everything that makes it work and do what is expected of it. This includes the web server software, logging in software (Active Directory LDAP etc) and the security softwares used to keep it running and free of virus and bad guys.

Networking. Switches, routers, all the cabling in a five building campus for me, wireless access, etc.

Phones, oh god the phone. I am not a fan of telephone infrastructure as we have VoIP phones, analog phones, fax machines, inter-building paging and intercom systems, old copper wiring from the 70's, fiber cable some brand new and some from the '00s. Some of these systems are going to be replaced which means that everyone who has a phone and phone number has an opinion on how that system should work and why are you IT guys not listening to my crazy ideas! (sorry ranted a bit).

Datacenters. We hired a guy to help design the rooms that the servers sit in, so that we could save on energy, cooling, HVAC etc. The guy we hired eventually stayed on and became a member of the server team. Our desktop guys change filters etc in the two datacenters we run.

Desktops, laptops, computers, cell phones. This is a whole team. These guys test the software we use with the Operating systems available, put the plans together to upgrade, support office applications and out management softwares, make and implement builds for the high end users, replace parts that fail in everything but the servers, are the antivirus people, and also train people on how to use office, photoshop, powerpoints and software like that.

Then you have people who write software, people who design web sites and web applications. These guys are a whole separate group that are considered "production" while I am considered "Infrastructure" along with the building and fleet maintenance people.

All of this is IT work. A friend works in a hospital and works on just about everything that plugs into a wall. He fixed a refrigerator for storing drugs, and has to support the doctors and nurses personal cell phones.

The sort answer here is honestly... whatever they pay you to do.

No problem. IT is a weird job in some of the ways. Some of my coworkers hold us responsible for all that has a screen, or every wireless device and everything that plugs into the wall. We have some users who demand we fix their personal computers, which we do when we have the time for 70$/hour. Never ever work for free. Ever. You get used to it if you are not careful. A small IT shop will do everything and anything that needs to be fixed, updated, repaired, configured, hit with the hammer. A bigger shop may force you into a cubicle and have a very certain job and nothing but that job.

My advice to all young people is to do as much as you can, as varied as you can while figuring out a specialty that you can be very highly talented in. The guy with a CCIE may get the job, but the networking guy who also knows enough VMWare to deploy servers and updates will be kept if their are layoffs in the future.

Hi, and welcome. If you've stumbled across this sub, you've probably noticed that it's yet new and unrefined. The first thing I thought would be wise to do is determine what exactly should be the scope of something as seemingly broad as "steampunk", and a good place to start is asking the people who ostensibly would make up a community interested in it.

Is steampunk a body of literature? If so, is it only that literature that includes Analytical or Difference Engines? Does it have to have a retro-futuristic bent or a narrow focus on outdated technology?

Or is steampunk a modern trend in fashion? Part of what prompted me to create this subverse was mounting frustration that its counterpart on Reddit had (at least as of the last time I visited) devolved into a series of pictures of pretty girls with gears on their clothes. If steampunk is fashion, is function a requirement?

If it's both, or better yet, if it's both and more, then what are its defining features? On what basis would you include or exclude a body of work or a piece of art?

Over the coming days I will be working to customize the sub (to the best of my limited abilities) and begin finding content that captures my interests and tastes. Of course, I'm but one person, so I'm very interested to hear the thoughts of other fans of the genre, whatever you conceive it to be.

Thanks!

When I was first introduced to steampunk, what I understood was that it was a way of building/engineering modern technology using 18th(ish) century Western aesthetics/materials/design. The fashion followed suit. Anything you created should have a purpose or function (or at least look like it did), not just sticking gears on stuff at random.

From my perspective, it's evolved to include industrial elements, goth inspirations, different timelines, bits of the fantastical, etc. Maybe there are purists out there, but I think having a bunch of choices makes for a better creative pursuit, as long as the crossover is heavier on the steampunk side.

As far as literature, there are definitely works out there that take inspiration from steampunk, but steampunk is not solely written word.

Hello everybody! I'm looking for other anthro artists, writers, animators and other kinds of creative people for what I like to call "a global community project".

But what is this project? It's a furry fantasy universe called "Planet Nakti".

Planet Nakti has the ambition to become the first furry universe that is developed entirely by the community. It mustn't be made only by one person, but with the contribution of everybody, with their ideas, skills and creativity, it could become a truly awesome project.

Nakti can be expanded with artworks, stories, animations, poems, games, roleplay and whatever you have in mind. You can create a Naktian character, a race, or a civilization with its traditions, customs, religions, history and many other things. There is total freedom in the development, only a few guidelines are required to be followed in order to not make the Naktian project into a carbon-copy of planet Earth or avoid copyright infringement (using characters from existing franchises and trademarked franchises is strictly forbidden! By the Gods be original!)

The most particular aspect of planet Nakti, is that it's a young planet, so its civilizations have a very early grade of technological development. They basically live in the same way we Earthlings lived during the age of the Ancient Egyptians or the Sumerians, so their technology is quite limited, and they don't have magic, because the characteristic of Nakti is that it's imbued with realism in mind, making it something that can really exist in another solar system.

Myself, I'm working on one of the Naktian countries, the Kingdom of Abun. :)

So, I'm looking for other artists who can join me and my friends who are already working on it, in this creative adventure, with the hope to unite all the anthros of the world together and making something that can really be considered a truly global effort.

If you are interested to join the project, please feel free to drop me a note. I look forward to answer all your questions. :3
